prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which has taken the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Having read the whole first-round exchange, I stay with the optical lattice clock, and with more conviction than in round 1, because the discussion answered the objection I was most worried about. I put the physics this way: Katori's magic-wavelength idea cancels the lattice light shift so that very many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and this is a different physical system with a different error budget from both the 2005 frequency comb and the 2012 single-ion control. The result is an instrument that asks nature direct questions: redshift across a millimetre, limits on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter. As Secretary I always ask first whether this is a discovery that is truly groundbreaking, and only then who stands behind it. Here the clocks are reproduced near 1e-18 by several independent laboratories and in several species, and that is the kind of confirmation that a prize can rest on. On the credit, Katori is the originator of the concept and the first realisation, and Ye took the clock to record accuracy and stability and showed that many-body effects belong to its physics. I would be more worried if either name were dropped than about how to weigh them against each other. That is a configuration of two people with a clear scientific logic, and I do not think a second prize part adds anything that can be defended.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. First, the chronology (Katori's 2003 proposal and the first strontium lattice clock around 2005, then Ye's group's records in later years) is something I and most of my colleagues are recalling from memory, not from primary papers, and the chair is right to say that convergence on a name is not verification. Second, Lemonde, Takamoto and the Yb and Hg groups have legitimate claims to a share of the lineage, and with two names the committee will pass over contributors that parts of the community consider essential. Third, a purist can still say that this is an extraordinary measurement capability rather than a discovery about nature, and my own scepticism toward elegant constructions that are not tested by nature does not apply here only because the lattice clock is itself such a test. If the citation is worded loosely around clocks in general, the 2005 and 2012 objection becomes easy to state. Finally, I still believe that EHT and IceCube are in some sense more existentially striking, and I am knowingly trading some of that for defensibility.

responses.point: She asks that the committee check the chronology against the 2003 to 2005 papers and says the record favours Katori on priority, with Ye's contribution being the 10^-18 accuracy and the many-body demonstration.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of her argument and I would add that it is exactly the kind of statement the Secretary's office should test, not assume. My own recollection is the same as hers: the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock come from Katori's group, while the JILA strontium clocks and the systematic-uncertainty and stability records came later and are Ye's. I cannot verify this from primary papers in this room, so I would propose that we state in the minutes that the credit split rests on that recollection, and that it be checked by an outside expert report before the final vote is treated as safe. I also would not read the priority difference as a hierarchy between the two: the citation says invention and development, and that is precisely a two-part contribution.

responses.point: He argues against waiting for the redefinition of the second, since a redefinition is a consequence of the clocks and not a test of them, and he warns that waiting risks a missed or contested attribution as the field grows.
responses.response: In round 1 I listed timing as open. I now side with him and change that position. The physics is already confirmed by independent laboratories, and a metrological body's schedule is not a scientific criterion for us. His second point also persuades me, because every year the clock community grows, with new species and new groups, the clear two-name credit becomes harder to defend. I would only add that this does not mean the redefinition is irrelevant as evidence: it is a sign of how mature the technology is, and I would mention it in the committee text but not in the citation.

responses.point: He says the prior prizes help only if the citation is worded around the magic-wavelength lattice and the accuracy attained, not around clocks in general.
responses.response: I accept this and have changed my citation accordingly. In round 1 it ended with enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level, which could be read as a general statement about precision metrology. I now name the optical lattice clock itself, and the 10^-18 level is attached to the lattice clock as an achievement and not as the purpose of the prize. I would keep the many-body physics in the committee's own motivation, as Johansson and Kroll suggested, and not in the citation, where it would invite a debate about what part of the work it covers.

responses.point: He asks whether the clock is a discovery or only an instrumentation advance, and says the citation needs a precise sentence on Katori as originator and Ye as developer.
responses.response: I do not think the distinction is as sharp as the question suggests. The prize is for discoveries, but our tradition has a long list of awards in which a new instrument opened a new regime of nature, and the lattice clock belongs there because what it measures, the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, the stability of constants, perhaps ultralight dark matter, are things nature does not show us otherwise. It is also not an instrument alone: the many-body spin-exchange effects seen inside the clock were not anticipated and are physics. On the citation, I think invention and development already carries the Katori and Ye roles in two words, so I would resist adding more detail that tries to rank them.

responses.point: As chair he asks that a better-informed colleague argue if Lemonde or Takamoto is a decisive third contributor, and that the committee test chronology and credit claims taken from memory.
responses.response: I think his demand is correct and I would answer it for my part this way. Takamoto was Katori's collaborator on the first strontium lattice clock and belongs to the same group, so I read that as a claim inside the Katori credit, not a rival one. Lemonde and the Paris group made important contributions, but I know of no documented ground that is strong enough to displace Ye or Katori under the limit of three, and I would not add a third name merely to be generous. If an atomic physicist on the committee can show otherwise from primary papers, I want to hear it before the vote.

uncertainties: The chronology of Katori's 2003 proposal and first strontium lattice clock against Ye's later accuracy and stability records, which I and most other members are recalling from memory and which has not been checked against primary papers or an external expert report.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd or Hollberg have a claim that is strong enough to alter the two-name credit, which I believe is not the case but cannot document.
Whether the committee as a whole accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the citation as worded keeps the ion-clock community outside it.
Whether IceCube (B033) would, after another year of results on the origin of the diffuse flux, become a cleaner case than the clock, which is why I keep it as the first alternative.
statement.conflict_note: I have no specific conflict with Katori, Ye or anyone credited in the preferred configuration, and I report no tie to the groups in the alternatives either. My supervisor David Gross and my collaborator Thomas Van Riet are not connected to any shortlisted candidate. My theoretical interest in black holes and cosmology is an intellectual preference for B052 and not a personal tie, and I have reduced its weight in my own ranking. I have read the disclosures of Johansson (B001), Eriksson (2025 chair), Kroll (Boulder), and Olsson (Tokyo) and see none that touches the B048 configuration; as Secretary I think they should be minuted, and I would follow the chair's view on any recusal if B001 returned.
